covers.quote: Use a comma after introductory words, such as greetings and adverbs, or when addressing someone.
You don’t need a comma after an introductory word if the sentence is very short.

parts.quote: Yes, they went to the estimates hearing.

examples.note: Greeting followed by a comma.

parts.quote: Today I went to work.

rules.quote: Place a comma after adverbs and other introductory words
rules.specification: Introductory words such as greetings, adverbs or direct address should be followed by a comma, unless the sentence is very short (4 words or fewer).
rules.violation_condition: an introductory word (such as a greeting, adverb, or direct address) at the start of a sentence not followed by a comma
when: You don’t need a comma after an introductory word if the sentence is very short.
rules.why: G-1 treats child headings as rules; G-3 absorbs the short-sentence permission under when; G-4 consolidates the restatement.

covers.quote: Use a comma after phrases and clauses that change the whole sentence
They should also have a comma after them if they start the sentence.

examples.note: Introductory adverbial phrase followed by a comma.

parts.quote: During the meeting, we discussed item 9.

examples.note: Introductory adverbial clause followed by a comma.

parts.quote: Although they were shaking and sweating, the firefighters were relieved to feel the first drops of a downpour.

examples.note: Introductory conditional clause followed by a comma.

parts.quote: Unless the consultation starts early, it will not finish on time.

rules.quote: Use commas after adverbial phrases and adverbial clauses.
rules.violation_condition: an introductory adverbial phrase or clause that starts a sentence without being followed by a comma
when: Applies when the phrase or clause begins the sentence.
Conditional clauses (e.g. beginning with 'if', 'unless', 'until') that start the sentence should have a comma after them.
When an adverbial phrase is placed at the end of a sentence, a comma before it is not required.
rules.why: G-2 consolidates conditional clauses into adverbial clauses; the body sentence states the rule more clearly than the heading.

covers.quote: Use a comma after an introductory phrase that ends with a numeral and is immediately followed by another numeral.
Avoid this type of sentence structure because the string of numbers can be confusing.

examples.note: Sentence rewritten so numbers and dates are not juxtaposed at the beginning.

parts.quote: There were 16.5 million people enrolled to vote in Australian elections on 18 April 2019.

examples.note: Begins with a date followed immediately by a numeral.

parts.quote: On 18 April 2019, 16.5 million people were enrolled to vote in Australian elections.

rules.quote: Avoid beginning a sentence with a string of numbers and dates
rules.violation_condition: a sentence starting with a numeral or date immediately followed by another numeral
when: If used, a comma must be placed after the introductory phrase ending with a numeral immediately followed by another numeral.
rules.why: G-2 groups the requirement and avoidance of the confusing numerical juxtaposition into one check with Write this / Not this.

covers.quote: Set off non-essential clauses
Use commas around clauses that add information but aren’t essential to the meaning of the sentence.
Don’t use commas if the clause is essential for meaning.
Generally, if you can take out part of the sentence and it is still grammatically correct, it should be between a pair of commas.

rules.quote: Within a sentence, use a pair of commas to separate non-essential or supplementary information.

when: Applies when the information is non-essential to meaning and grammatical structure.
Do not use commas if the clause is essential to meaning.
rules.why: G-1 and G-2 consolidate setting off non-essential clauses into the rule on comma pairs for non-essential information.

covers.quote: Use commas with the phrase ‘for example’
If ‘for example’ begins a sentence, it is an introductory phrase. Follow it with a comma.
If you’re introducing a bullet list after ‘for example’, use a colon.

rules.quote: Generally, use a comma before and after the phrase ‘for example’ in a sentence.
rules.violation_condition: the phrase 'for example' used within a sentence without being enclosed in commas, or at the start of a sentence without a following comma

covers.quote: Place commas between principal clauses joined together with a conjunction
Use commas to connect 2 or more principal clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction (‘and’, ‘or’, ‘but’, ‘so’).
If 2 clauses share the same subject, you don’t need to repeat the subject or insert a comma before the conjunction.
The exception to this rule is when you have joined more than 2 principal clauses with the same subject.

examples.note: Comma before conjunction between clauses with different subjects.

parts.quote: The Senate debated the Bill at length, but the party whips eventually called for a vote.

examples.note: Shared subject requires no comma before 'and'.

examples.note: More than 2 principal clauses sharing the same subject separated by commas.

rules.quote: If they have different subjects, use a comma before the coordinating conjunction.
rules.violation_condition: two principal clauses with different subjects joined by a coordinating conjunction without a comma before the conjunction
when: If 2 clauses share the same subject, you don’t need to repeat the subject or insert a comma before the conjunction.
When joining more than 2 principal clauses with the same subject, use commas between them.
Do not use this rule to create a sentence of more than 25 words.
rules.why: G-2: one rule covering comma usage between coordinated principal clauses across different subject conditions.

covers.quote: Don’t use commas to ‘splice’ sentences

rules.quote: Don’t use a comma to link 2 stand-alone sentences unless you use a coordinating conjunction.
rules.violation_condition: two independent clauses joined only by a comma without a coordinating conjunction (comma splice)
rules.why: Distinct syntactic prohibition (comma splice) with explicit Correct and Incorrect examples.

covers.quote: Separate items in lists of nouns or adjectives with commas
Restrict the use of the Oxford comma
If the last item combines 2 words or phrases with the word ‘and’, use a comma before that final item.
Do not punctuate the end of a list item with a comma if it is in a bullet list.

rules.quote: Use commas between items in a sentence list. Avoid using a comma before the last item in the list.
rules.specification: Separate items in sentence lists with commas. Do not place a comma before the final 'and'/'or' unless the final item combines words with 'and' or an Oxford comma is needed to prevent ambiguity. Do not end bullet list items with commas.
rules.violation_condition: items in a sentence list not separated by commas, or an unnecessary Oxford comma before 'and' when not needed for ambiguity
when: Do not punctuate the end of a list item with a comma if it is in a bullet list.
If the last item combines 2 words or phrases with the word ‘and’, use a comma before that final item.
Use the Oxford comma before the last item if using a defining phrase applicable only to that final item or to prevent ambiguity in complex lists.
rules.why: G-2: Oxford comma conditions qualify when the serial comma is permitted or avoided in sentence lists.

covers.quote: Use commas in numbers with 4 or more digits
Don’t use a space between the digits, because screen readers can read them as separate numbers.
When you are using numbers of 1,000 or more, use commas to separate the numerals into groups of 3 (working right to left).
Commas are not used to the right of a decimal point.
Don’t use commas in postcodes or dates.

when: Commas are not used to the right of a decimal point.

rules.why: G-2 gathers formatting of numbers of 4+ digits, space prohibitions, and date/postcode exceptions into one rule.

covers.quote: Show direct speech or quoted material using commas
If an attribution comes after a quotation, use a comma at the end of the quotation and before the quotation mark.
If the quotation is broken into 2 parts, the second part should follow a full stop rather than a comma.
If the quotation ends the sentence, end it with the original punctuation of the quotation.

examples.note: Oxford comma used to prevent ambiguity with defining phrase.

parts.quote: The analysis outlined demand for barley, wheat, and hay for stockfeed.

tags.specification: Separate items in sentence lists with commas. Do not place a comma before the final 'and'/'or' unless the final item combines words with 'and' or an Oxford comma is needed to prevent ambiguity. Do not end bullet list items with commas.
tags.violation_condition: items in a sentence list not separated by commas, or an unnecessary Oxford comma before 'and' when not needed for ambiguity

when: Do not punctuate the end of a list item with a comma if it is in a bullet list.
If the last item combines 2 words or phrases with the word ‘and’, use a comma before that final item.
Use the Oxford comma before the last item if using a defining phrase applicable only to that final item or to prevent ambiguity in complex lists.
rules.why: G-2: Oxford comma conditions qualify when the serial comma is permitted or avoided in sentence lists.

anchor.quote: Use commas in strings of adjectives of the same type (for example, a string of descriptive adjectives).

covers.quote: Separate adjectives of the same type
Don’t use commas in strings of adjectives of different types.

examples.note: Commas separating descriptive adjectives of the same type.

parts.quote: This is an ethical, profitable, efficient organisation.

examples.note: Commas separating evaluative adjectives of the same type.

parts.quote: They were a happy, caring, devoted workforce.

examples.note: No commas between adjectives of different types.

parts.quote: We found some used French tennis balls left over from a training day.

tags.violation_condition: adjectives of the same type in a string not separated by commas, or adjectives of different types separated by commas

when: Don’t use commas in strings of adjectives of different types.
rules.why: G-2 combines positive and negative rules on adjective strings.

anchor.quote: Numbers with 4 or more digits (starting from 1,000) need a comma. Use commas for numerals in text and in tables.

covers.quote: Use commas in numbers with 4 or more digits
Don’t use a space between the digits, because screen readers can read them as separate numbers.
When you are using numbers of 1,000 or more, use commas to separate the numerals into groups of 3 (working right to left).
Commas are not used to the right of a decimal point.
Don’t use commas in postcodes or dates.

examples.note: Four-digit number formatted with a comma.

parts.quote: The agency handles around 6,500 complaints each year.

examples.note: Space used instead of a comma.

parts.quote: The agency handles around 6 500 complaints each year.
parts.suffix: [This can be read as the number

examples.note: Comma used left of decimal, no comma to the right.
Year written without a comma.

parts.quote: The year was 2020.

examples.note: Postcode written without a comma.

parts.quote: The office was in postcode area 6500.

tags.violation_condition: a numeral of 4 or more digits written without a thousands separator comma, or written with a space instead of a comma

when: Commas are not used to the right of a decimal point.
Don’t use commas in postcodes or dates.
rules.why: G-2 gathers formatting of numbers of 4+ digits, space prohibitions, and date/postcode exceptions into one rule.

anchor.quote: Introduce directly quoted speech with a comma. Use the comma in combination with quotation marks.

covers.quote: Show direct speech or quoted material using commas
If an attribution comes after a quotation, use a comma at the end of the quotation and before the quotation mark.
If the quotation is broken into 2 parts, the second part should follow a full stop rather than a comma.
If the quotation ends the sentence, end it with the original punctuation of the quotation.

examples.note: Direct speech introduced with a comma.

parts.quote: She said, ‘It’s time to start work.’

examples.note: Attribution following quotation with comma inside quote.

parts.quote: ‘It’s time to start work,’ she said.

examples.note: Broken quotation where second part follows a full stop.

parts.quote: ‘It’s time to start work,’ she said. ‘We have a lot to do.’

tags.violation_condition: directly quoted speech introduced without a comma before the opening quotation mark, or an attribution following a quotation without a comma preceding the closing quotation mark

when: If an attribution comes after a quotation, use a comma at the end of the quotation and before the quotation mark.
If the quotation is broken into 2 parts, the second part should follow a full stop rather than a comma.
If the quotation ends the sentence, end it with the original punctuation of the quotation.
rules.why: G-2 groups rules for punctuate attributions and quoted speech into one coherent rule.
